items.stem: An input accepts integers from 1 to 100. Which set of values best reflects boundary-value analysis?

options.rationale: Correct: boundary-value analysis tests just inside and just outside each limit.
A single mid-range value tests neither boundary.
Random mid-range values are unlikely to probe the boundaries where defects cluster.
Testing just the valid edges omits the just-outside values that catch off-by-one errors.

items.explanation: Correct: boundary-value analysis tests just inside and just outside each limit.

items.stem: Why is 90% code coverage not proof that software is correct?

options.text: Coverage shows which lines ran, not whether their behaviour was verified
options.rationale: Correct: executing a line is not the same as asserting it produced the right result for all relevant cases.

options.text: Coverage above 80% is always sufficient by standard
options.rationale: No standard threshold proves correctness; the limitation is conceptual.
Coverage can be measured at any test level; that is not the issue.
Coverage says nothing specific about boundary conditions.

items.explanation: Correct: executing a line is not the same as asserting it produced the right result for all relevant cases.

items.stem: Which TWO statements reflect a healthy application of the test pyramid? (Select TWO)

options.text: Many fast unit tests form the base of the suite
options.rationale: Correct: a broad base of fast unit tests gives quick, stable feedback.

options.text: Fewer, slower end-to-end tests sit at the top
options.rationale: Correct: expensive end-to-end tests are used sparingly for critical flows.

options.text: Most tests should be slow end-to-end UI tests
options.rationale: A top-heavy suite is the ice-cream-cone anti-pattern: slow and brittle.

options.text: Unit tests should be avoided to save time
options.rationale: Unit tests are the most cost-effective layer, not something to avoid.

items.explanation: Correct: a broad base of fast unit tests gives quick, stable feedback.
